name: Zane Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I like talking about work, as long as nobody from the firm reads it with my name on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter on the formwork crew at the hospital extension on Mill Road. Formwork is the timber and steel moulds you pour concrete into, so I build the boxes for columns and slab edges, then strip them once the concrete's set. The firm's a big contractor, so there's a proper canteen and a toolbox talk at half seven every morning. I like seeing a column come out clean; I don't like stripping ply off at three in the afternoon when your back's gone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Priya; she's a nursing assistant at the old hospital, the one we're building the extension for, funnily enough. We rent a terrace with damp in the back bedroom. We've got about three weeks of money saved, and she earns a bit more than me, which my dad still teases me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe the hype was the robots we didn't need. At work I'd say the same and maybe ask why the site office bought all those tablets. Online I'd share something saying the money should've gone into wages and housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same deal as now. The hospital job runs another fourteen months, and the firm usually moves its formwork lads to the next big pour. If they don't, there's nothing round here but small builders paying cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, work the overtime when they offer it, and keep my union card paid up. I use the chatbot now and then to explain a drawing detail, and I'd still do that. I'd also try to get my level two carpentry certificate finished, because I'm halfway through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, maybe, because nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm usually moves its formwork lads on. What if they don't this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm on the phone to every small builder in a thirty-mile radius. Last time there was a gap, two years back, I did six weeks of labouring for a roofer who paid late. That's when Priya and I started keeping a jar for the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to change in a world where nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents, honestly. We pay more for a damp terrace than my parents paid for their mortgage. AI being a flop doesn't touch that.

say: I'd say the money should've gone into **wages and housing**, not hype.
I'd ask at work why the site office bought **all those tablets**.
think: The **hospital job** runs fourteen more months and the firm usually moves formwork lads on.
If it doesn't, the only local work is **small builders** paying cash.
do: Work the **overtime** when offered and keep his **union card** paid.
Finish his **level two** carpentry certificate, which is half done.
Keep using the **chatbot** now and then to explain drawing details.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but **flat**, because nothing gets better either.
S0.quote: We pay more for a damp terrace than my parents paid for their mortgage.
fieldNote: His job feels **safe for now** because a big contractor carries him.
A past **six-week gap** taught him how thin things get.
His real grievance is **rent**, not technology.
He uses AI **casually** for reading drawings, without much thought.

steps.text: Take the overtime on the hospital extension pours
Finish the second half of his level two carpentry certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where unions earn their money. On site I'd tell the lads the office will shrink first and we need to make sure the savings don't just go to shareholders. Online I'd share stuff about a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly fine for me for a while. Formwork's heavy and messy, every pour's a bit different, and robots are years off doing it. What worries me is the firm using AI to plan us tighter, fewer lads per pour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the planning app properly instead of just ticking boxes, because the lads who understand it get made chargehand. I'd finish the certificate this year. And I'd put fifty a month into savings, which sounds small but it's more than we manage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Like when the gaffer starts walking round with a clipboard counting heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer lads per pour. Who goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency lads, then the juniors who are slow. I'm junior but I'm not slow anymore, so I'd hope I'm in the middle. My mate Ollie is agency and he'd be gone first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to Ollie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his name on the firm's books proper, not agency, while they're still hiring for the hospital. I'd lend him my certificate notes. That's about all I can do.

say: I'd say this is where **unions earn** their money.
I'd push for the office savings to fund a **shorter week**, not shareholders.
think: **Formwork** is heavy and messy, so robots are years off doing it.
The real risk is AI planning crews **tighter**, with fewer lads per pour.
do: Learn the **planning app** properly, since those who understand it become chargehand.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the gaffer walking round counting heads with a clipboard.
S1.quote: Formwork's heavy and messy, every pour's a bit different, and robots are years off doing it.
fieldNote: He judges his own **hands-on job** as safe for now and is mostly right.
He sees AI arriving as **tighter planning**, not as a robot.
He worries for **agency workers** like his friend more than himself.
He's willing to learn tech **once it pays**, like a chargehand role.

steps.text: Learn the site planning app to aim for chargehand
Finish the carpentry certificate this year
Save fifty a month in a separate account
Back union calls for a shorter week from office savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency and we need a wealth tax yesterday. At work I'd say the hands-on lads have three years, so use them. Online I'd be the one posting long angry threads, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in real trouble by 2031. I'd have no house, three weeks of savings, and a certificate in the one thing robots are coming for next. Priya's job might hold, because people want a human holding their hand in hospital, but we can't live on her pay alone with this rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd move fast: get the certificate, then try to get onto the robot side, maybe as the lad who sets up and checks the machines on site. I'd use the AI tools every day to learn, not just now and then. And I'd join the union campaign for a basic income, properly, door knocking and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I've been running for a bus and just watched it pull away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Priya's job might hold. How would you feel about relying on her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about it in theory, I'm not old-fashioned. In practice I'd hate it, because she already does the hard shifts. I'd feel like I was on the sofa while she held everything up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different in those three years between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site office would empty out, the planners and buyers, so the bosses would be squeezing every hour out of us. Three years between AGI and the robots means three years of dread with a nail gun, working harder for the same money. And the whole time you'd know the robots were coming.

say: I'd call it a **political emergency** and demand a wealth tax.
I'd tell the lads the hands-on crews have **three years** to use well.
think: By **2031** he'd have no house, thin savings and a certificate robots can copy.
His partner's **hospital job** may hold, but one wage can't cover the rent.
do: Finish the certificate, then aim to **set up and check** site robots.
Use **AI tools daily** to learn instead of now and then.
Door-knock for the union's **basic income** campaign.
feel: Like **watching the bus** he was running for pull away.
S2.quote: Three years between AGI and the robots means three years of dread with a nail gun, working harder for the same money.
fieldNote: He expects **2028–2031** to bring harder work, not job loss, then loss.
Relying on his **partner's wage** clashes with his pride though he denies it.
He'd switch from casual to **daily AI use** to stay ahead.
His politics turn **active**: campaigning, not just posting.

steps.text: Train to set up and check robots on building sites
Use AI tools every day to study for new roles
Door-knock for the union's basic income campaign
Lean on his partner's hospital wage if site work goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's not waste it like we wasted the last warnings. At work I'd push the union to get a deal on retraining written in. Online, same as ever, wealth tax, shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think with five years plus three, I've got a fighting chance. That's long enough to finish my papers and get into something like site supervision or machine setup. But I'd be doing it on three weeks of savings, which is the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the certificate and start the supervisor's course at the college, evenings. I'd learn the AI planning tools properly, because supervisors will be the ones driving them. And Priya and I would push the wedding back a couple of years to save instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I can see a path. It's like a steep ladder rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pushing back the wedding. How would Priya take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably say she was going to suggest it. Her mum would be the upset one. We'd still do the registry office, just not the big do with two hundred cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is supervision really safe if AI can do almost any thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not totally, no, you've got me there. But somebody still has to stand on the slab and make the call when the concrete truck's late. I'd rather be that person than the one being replaced.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** we shouldn't waste like the last ones.
I'd push the union to **write in** a retraining deal.
think: **Eight years** gives him a fighting chance at supervision or machine setup.
Doing it on **three weeks** of savings is what keeps him awake.
do: Start the **supervisor's course** at evening college after finishing the certificate.
Learn the **AI planning tools** properly, since supervisors will drive them.
Push the **wedding** back two years and save instead.
feel: **Nervous** but hopeful, like a **steep ladder** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Somebody still has to stand on the slab and make the call when the concrete truck's late.
fieldNote: The **extra two years** shift him from alarm to a workable plan.
He concedes **supervision** isn't fully safe but still prefers it.
Postponing the **big wedding** is his main family trade-off.
Savings, not skill, are his **weak point**.

steps.text: Start the evening site supervisor's course at the college
Learn the AI planning tools supervisors use
Move the big wedding back two years and keep the registry office
Push the union for a written retraining deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a decent government to plan this, so judge them on whether they do. At work I'd say let's train now. Online I'd probably calm down a bit, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until robots, I'd be forty. That's a career. I could get to supervisor, or into setting up machines, and still have time to save a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, same start: finish the certificate, then the supervisor's course. I'd keep the union involved. I'd also start using AI for my study more, but I wouldn't rush, because with ten years you can wait and see what actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still a bit of fear in the background, like weather on the forecast for next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still be anxious. About what, if there's so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mostly, and that the government wastes the decade. I've seen councils take ten years to fix one roundabout. It's not the robots, it's whether anyone uses the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a sixteen-year-old starting on the site today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your papers early, learn the machines, and don't let anyone tell you the hands-on lads are safe forever. And join the union on your first day. I wish someone had told me at sixteen.

say: I'd say voters should judge government on whether it **uses ten years** to plan.
I'd tell people at work to **start training** now.
think: **Thirteen years** to robots means a real career for him.
He could reach **supervisor** or machine setup and still save a **deposit**.
do: Finish the certificate and then the **supervisor's course**.
Keep the **union** involved in any training deal.
Use AI for study more but **wait and see** which tools work.
feel: **Steadier**, with fear in the background like **bad weather** forecast for next week.
S4.quote: I've seen councils take ten years to fix one roundabout.
fieldNote: His fear moves from robots to **wasted time** by government.
**Rent** keeps the mood above uneasy despite the long runway.
He'd **slow down** on AI adoption when time allows.
His advice to the young is **papers, machines, union**.

steps.text: Finish the certificate and then the supervisor's course
Keep pressing the union to shape training deals
Hold off on new AI tools until crews show which work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The three years between the computers and the robots would be the worst bit, squeezed harder while you wait for the axe. What would help is a retraining wage, so you can study without losing the flat, and a union seat when firms buy the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about housing. Every answer I gave comes back to rent, because if rent were sane I'd have a cushion and none of this would scare me as much.

headlineQuote: If rent were sane I'd have a cushion and none of this would scare me as much.
portrait: Zane is **27**, a junior formwork carpenter on a hospital extension, with about **three weeks** saved.
He's **pro-union**, uses AI now and then, and blames high **rent** for most of his stress.
He sees his **hands-on job** as safe in mild scenarios but expects tighter crews.
AGI by **2028** alarms him; he'd chase machine setup and campaign for a basic income.
With more time he plans **supervision** and moves his big wedding back to save.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, especially the squeezed **years** before robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining wage** so he can study without losing the flat.
A **union seat** when firms decide to buy robots.
